title: MAYBE GOD ISN’T SHOWING YOU THE WHOLE ROAD BECAUSE HE’S ASKING YOU TO TRUST HIM WITH THE NEXT STEP.
paragraphs: MAYBE GOD ISN’T SHOWING YOU THE WHOLE ROAD BECAUSE HE’S ASKING YOU TO TRUST HIM WITH THE NEXT STEP.
You keep asking Jesus to show you what happens next. But what if the breakthrough in your faith begins when you finally obey Him without knowing how the story ends?
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
It comes from standing at the edge of a decision you know you cannot avoid, praying for an answer that never seems complete.
You have asked God for clarity.
You have asked Him for confirmation.
You have whispered, sometimes through tears, “Lord, just show me what is going to happen. I promise I will follow You. I just need to know where this is going.”
But the full explanation never comes.
And now you are caught between two fears.
You are afraid to move because you do not know what lies ahead.
And you are afraid to stay because somewhere deep inside, you wonder whether your fear has become an excuse for delaying what God has already made clear.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still read your Bible, even if some days you barely have the strength.
You still pray, even when your prayers sound more like questions than declarations of faith.
But you are tired of not knowing.
Tired of wondering whether the opportunity will work out.
Whether the relationship will survive.
Whether your family will be okay.
Whether the money will be enough.
Whether the healing will come.
Whether the decision you are considering will become the beginning of something beautiful or another chapter you will have to recover from.
And perhaps the question you are most afraid to say out loud is this:
“Jesus, if I really am following You, why does the road still feel so uncertain?”
If that question has ever lived in your heart, I want you to stay with me.
Because there is a man in Scripture who walked into an unknown future with nothing resembling the guarantees we so desperately want.
And what God teaches us through his life may change the way you understand the uncertainty you are facing right now.
His name was Abraham.
And his story did not begin with a complete explanation.
It began with a call.
Hebrews 11:8 says:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.” — Hebrews 11:8, KJV
Read those final words again.
“Not knowing whither he went.”
Not knowing.
He did not possess the entire itinerary.
He did not have a detailed map of every difficulty waiting for him.
He did not know every person he would encounter, every disappointment he would endure, or every moment when the promise would appear impossibly distant.
Yet Scripture tells us something remarkable.
He obeyed.
In the original Greek of Hebrews 11:8, we find these words:
Πίστει καλούμενος Ἀβραὰμ ὑπήκουσεν
Pistei kaloumenos Abraam hypēkousen.
“By faith, Abraham, when called, obeyed.”
The word πίστει (pistei) means “by faith.” It is a form of pistis, the Greek word commonly translated as faith, trust, or belief.
And ὑπήκουσεν (hypēkousen) means “he obeyed.”
The writer then describes Abraham as going out:
μὴ ἐπιστάμενος ποῦ ἔρχεται
Mē epistamenos pou erchetai.
“Not knowing where he was going.”
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say Abraham understood everything, and therefore he obeyed.
It does not say he received answers to every possible question.
It says he was called, he obeyed, and he went without knowing his destination.
His obedience was not the result of possessing complete information.
It was a response of faith to the God who called him.
And that distinction matters more than we sometimes realize.
Because some of us have quietly made an agreement with God that sounds spiritual but may actually be keeping us from trusting Him.
“Lord, I will obey when I understand.”
“I will forgive when I know they will never hurt me again.”
“I will take the righteous path when I can see how it will benefit me.”
“I will surrender this relationship when You show me what will replace it.”
“I will stop compromising when I know I will not lose anything.”
“I will follow You completely when my future feels secure.”
And Jesus, in His mercy, confronts the condition we have placed on our obedience.
Not because He enjoys watching us struggle.
Not because asking questions is sinful.
Not because wisdom, planning, and discernment are unnecessary.
But because trust that demands complete control is not the same thing as faith.
That is difficult to hear when uncertainty has already cost you so much.
Especially if you have obeyed before and still experienced heartbreak.
Maybe you did what was right, and someone betrayed you anyway.
Maybe you prayed over a decision, sought godly counsel, and still found yourself walking through a painful season.
Maybe you stepped away from something sinful, only to discover that obedience did not immediately make life easier.
You expected peace to mean that everything would settle down.
Instead, the storm continued.
And somewhere along the way, you began confusing God's faithfulness with the absence of difficulty.
But Abraham's story will not allow us to make that assumption.
The man who obeyed God still experienced waiting.
He still faced famine.
He still made serious mistakes.
He still struggled with the enormous distance between what God had promised and what his circumstances appeared to say.
Genesis 12:10 tells us there was a famine in the land.
Think about that.
Abraham followed God's call, arrived in the land of promise, and encountered a famine.
The presence of hardship did not automatically mean he had followed the wrong God.
And the presence of a divine promise did not mean every choice Abraham made afterward was wise or faithful.
In fact, Genesis records his failures with striking honesty.
Abraham was not a flawless spiritual hero who never trembled.
He was a man who needed the mercy of the God he was learning to trust.
That should encourage every believer who has ever whispered, “Lord, I believe, but I am still afraid.”
Faith is not pretending you have no questions.
Faith is not denying the reality of suffering.
Faith is not calling every impulse a divine instruction and expecting God to bless it.
Biblical faith receives God's Word as trustworthy and responds to Him, even when the outcome remains beyond our sight.
And sometimes that response is not a dramatic relocation, a career change, or a leap into the unknown.
Sometimes it is something far more personal.
It is finally telling the truth.
It is ending a pattern of dishonesty that has been quietly destroying your integrity.
It is refusing to return to a relationship built on manipulation, even though loneliness frightens you.
It is apologizing without knowing whether the other person will forgive you.
It is seeking help because you can no longer pretend everything is fine.
It is choosing holiness when compromise would be easier.
It is opening your Bible again after months of spiritual numbness.
It is praying, “Jesus, I do not understand what You are doing, but I know what You have already commanded me to do.”
And then doing that thing.
Not to earn His love.
Not to purchase His favor.
Not to prove that you are stronger than everyone else.
But because you belong to the One who loved you first.
There is another detail in Abraham's story that deserves our attention.
When God called Abram in Genesis 12:1, the command included these words in Hebrew:
לֶךְ־לְךָ
Lekh-lekha.
“Go,” or “go forth.”
The expression introduces God's command for Abram to leave his country, his kindred, and his father's house for the land God would show him.
And the Hebrew text continues:
אֶל־הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ
El-ha'aretz asher ar'ekka.
“To the land that I will show you.”
God identified Himself as the One who would show Abraham the land.
He did not give Abraham every detail before the journey began.
The promise was anchored in God's word, not Abraham's ability to predict the future.
And perhaps that is where your heart has been struggling.
You want to see enough of tomorrow to feel safe today.
You want to know that your obedience will not cost you too much.
You want the assurance that if you surrender what God is asking you to surrender, you will never regret it.
But Jesus never promised His followers a life without suffering.
He promised something infinitely greater than a comfortable life.
He promised Himself.
And that brings us to the part of this story we cannot afford to miss.
Because Abraham's faith is not ultimately a lesson about becoming brave enough to achieve our dreams.
It belongs to the larger story of God's redemption.
God promised Abraham that through him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3).
The New Testament reveals the fulfillment of that blessing in Jesus Christ.
Galatians 3:8 connects God's promise to Abraham with the Gospel being announced beforehand.
Galatians 3:16 directs our attention to Christ, the promised offspring.
And Galatians 3:29 declares that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise.
Do you see what that means?
The God who called Abraham into an unknown future was already unfolding a redemptive purpose far greater than Abraham could have comprehended.
And at the center of that purpose stood Jesus.
Not merely as an inspiring example of courage.
Not merely as a teacher who encourages us to take risks.
But as the Savior who would bear our sins, conquer death, and bring sinners into the family of God through grace.
That is why this message must never become another motivational speech about believing in yourself.
The Gospel is not that you can accomplish anything if you take the first step. The Gospel is that Jesus Christ has accomplished what you could never accomplish to save yourself.
You cannot obey your way into forgiveness.
You cannot perform enough acts of faith to erase your guilt.
You cannot become righteous before God by collecting impressive testimonies.
Ephesians 2:8–9 tells us that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works.
And the very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Then a transformed life follows.
We do not obey to make Jesus love us.
We learn to obey because, in Christ, we have encountered the love that saves and changes us.
And if you are struggling with uncertainty right now, there is something about the cross that you need to remember.
Think about the disciples on the day Jesus was crucified.
They had followed Him.
They had heard His teaching.
They had witnessed His miracles.
They had seen the blind receive sight, the sick restored, and the dead raised.
Yet when Jesus was arrested, condemned, and crucified, their expectations collapsed.
The One they believed to be the Messiah was hanging on a Roman cross.
From their limited perspective, everything appeared to be falling apart.
Luke 24:21 records the heartbreaking words of two disciples on the road to Emmaus:
“But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel.” — KJV
Listen to the grief in that sentence.
“We trusted.”
Past tense.
They were speaking as though their hope had died.
And yet the risen Jesus was walking with them.
They could not recognize Him at first.
They could not yet understand how the Scriptures pointed to His suffering and glory.
They could not see that the event they interpreted as the destruction of their hope was central to God's saving purpose.
The cross was not the defeat of God's plan.
It was the place where the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And the resurrection was God's triumphant vindication of His Son.
But be careful here.
This does not mean every painful event in your life will eventually reveal itself to be a hidden blessing.
It does not mean every relationship will be restored.
It does not mean every diagnosis will end in physical healing during this life.
It does not mean every financial loss will be followed by greater wealth.
And it certainly does not mean that God approves of the evil people have done to you.
What the cross and resurrection do tell us is that our limited understanding cannot measure the limits of God's power, wisdom, or faithfulness.
If God can bring salvation through the death and resurrection of His Son, then you have reason to trust His character even when you cannot explain your circumstances.
Not because you know what tomorrow will bring.
But because you know who Jesus is.
And perhaps that is the invitation before you today.
Not to figure out your entire future.
Not to force open a door that God has not opened.
Not to manufacture a sign out of every coincidence.
Not to make an impulsive decision simply because someone told you that real faith never hesitates.
But to bring your uncertainty honestly before the Lord and ask:
“Jesus, what have You already made clear in Your Word that I have been afraid to obey?”
That question can be uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we are not waiting for guidance.
We are resisting guidance we have already received.
We know we need to repent.
We know we need to stop lying.
We know we need to release bitterness.
We know we need to turn away from the sin we keep defending.
We know we need to love the person we have been treating with contempt.
We know we need to stop building our identity around human approval.
And instead of obeying, we keep asking God to reveal the next ten years.
But there are other times when the decision genuinely is unclear.
The Bible may tell you to act with integrity, but it may not tell you which of two honest jobs to accept.
It may tell you to love wisely, but it may not reveal whether a particular relationship will lead to marriage.
It may tell you to care for your family, but it may not provide a detailed financial plan.
In those moments, obedience does not mean pretending you heard a specific command from God when you did not.

It means walking within the truth He has revealed, praying for wisdom, seeking mature counsel, examining your motives, considering the consequences, and making responsible decisions without demanding certainty that no human being possesses.
James 1:5 encourages believers to ask God for wisdom.
Proverbs 15:22 recognizes the value of counsel.
And Proverbs 3:5–6 calls us to trust in the Lord rather than lean entirely on our own understanding.
These truths belong together.
Trusting God is not abandoning wisdom.
It is refusing to make our limited understanding the final authority over His revealed truth.
And there is something else you need to hear.
You are allowed to be afraid.
Abraham's example does not require you to become emotionally invincible.
The Psalms are filled with faithful people crying out in distress.
David asked questions.
Jeremiah lamented.
Job wrestled with suffering he could not explain.
Even in Gethsemane, Jesus, the sinless Son of God, expressed profound sorrow as He approached the suffering He would willingly endure.
Matthew 26:39 records His prayer:
“Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
Jesus was not uncertain about the Father's identity or the saving mission before Him.
His prayer reveals His genuine human anguish and His perfect submission to the Father's will.
And if you are His disciple, you do not have to disguise your trembling to come before Him.
You can pray with tears.
You can confess that you are afraid.
You can admit that you wish things were different.
You can ask for help.
Faith does not require you to become dishonest about your pain.
It calls you to bring that pain to the God who hears you.
Perhaps tonight you are staring at a ceiling while everyone else is asleep.
Your phone is beside you.
There are bills waiting.
Messages you have not answered.
A conversation you have been avoiding.
A decision that seems to grow heavier every day.
You have replayed every possible outcome until your mind feels like a room full of doors, and every door frightens you.
And maybe you opened this article hoping to find the exact answer to your situation.
I cannot promise that these words will tell you which job to take, which city to move to, or when your circumstances will change.
But I can point you to the Savior who has already revealed enough of His character for you to trust Him.
Jesus Christ is not asking you to save yourself by making a perfect decision.
He is calling you to trust Him, follow His truth, and receive the grace you desperately need.
And sometimes the next faithful step is much smaller than the enormous future you have been trying to solve.
It may be putting your phone down and praying instead of feeding your anxiety.
It may be asking forgiveness.
It may be making an appointment for the help you need.
It may be telling a trusted Christian friend what you have been hiding.
It may be choosing not to make a decision tonight because wisdom requires more information.
It may be finally doing the right thing that fear has persuaded you to postpone.
And yes, sometimes it may mean moving forward without knowing exactly how everything will unfold.
But hear this carefully.
Do not confuse an uncertain outcome with an uncertain Savior.
Your circumstances may change.
Your plans may fail.
People may disappoint you.
Your understanding may prove incomplete.
But Jesus Christ is not made less faithful by the things you cannot foresee.
Hebrews 13:8 declares:
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.” — KJV
That is where your confidence belongs.
Not in the perfection of your plans.
Not in the strength of your emotions.
Not in your ability to predict the future.
But in Christ.
The One who died for your sins.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who calls you to repentance and offers forgiveness.
The One whose grace is sufficient even when your courage feels painfully small.
And if you have spent years running from Him, perhaps the most important next step has nothing to do with your career, your relationship, or your financial future.
Perhaps it is finally surrendering your life to Jesus Christ.
You may have built an entire reputation around looking strong.
You may have convinced everyone that you are doing fine.
You may know how to quote Scripture while secretly living in disobedience.
You may be carrying guilt from decisions no one else knows about.
But you do not need to clean up your entire history before coming to the Savior.
You need to come to Him in repentance and faith.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we understood everything.
Not after we fixed every failure.
Christ died for sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
That the guilty can be forgiven.
That the spiritually dead can be made alive.
That the person who wasted years running from God can be welcomed through Jesus Christ.
That your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in faith.
This is why we keep returning to the words that define the heart of Gospel Warrior:
Not every painful chapter disappears.
Not every consequence is erased.
Not every broken relationship is restored exactly as it was.
But through Christ, sinners can become children of God, shame can give way to forgiveness, and a life once ruled by darkness can begin to bear the fruit of His transforming grace.
And that is a story worth telling.
Especially to the person who is afraid that it is already too late.
I want you to think of someone right now.
Someone who keeps saying, “I just don't know what to do anymore.”
Someone who has been waiting for certainty before taking a step toward Jesus.
Someone who has been spiritually exhausted by trying to control every outcome.
Someone who has mistaken a difficult season for proof that God has abandoned them.
Maybe it is your husband.
Your wife.
Your child.
Your parent.
Your closest friend.
Maybe it is someone who has stopped going to church because disappointment made faith feel too painful.
Maybe it is a person who does not yet believe in Jesus but is beginning to wonder whether there is hope beyond the life they have been living.
Not simply to increase the number of people who see it.
But because someone scrolling through their feed tonight may be carrying a burden they have never found the courage to explain.
A single shared message cannot solve every problem.
But it can place Scripture, hope, and the invitation of the Gospel before someone who needs to hear them.
And if this article has spoken to something you are personally facing, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
You do not have to explain every detail of your situation.
You do not have to expose something deeply private.
But perhaps your simple comment will become an encouragement to another believer who thought they were the only one wrestling with fear.
And if you need prayer, you can comment, “Pray for me. I'm learning to trust Jesus.”
There is no shame in admitting that faith is a daily struggle.
There is no shame in asking your brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you.
We were never called to walk the Christian life in isolation.
Return to Hebrews 11:8.
Read it slowly.
Remember Abraham.
Remember that the God who called him was faithful even when Abraham could not see the entire road.
And above all, remember Jesus.
Because your greatest hope is not that you will always take the correct step.
Your greatest hope is that you have a faithful Savior whose mercy is greater than your failures and whose Word remains true.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want to keep bringing people back to Scripture, back to repentance, back to grace, and back to the living hope found in Jesus Christ.
Not to create a following built around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell spiritual shortcuts.
But to help people open the Bible, understand the Gospel, and grow in a faith that reaches beyond a moment of inspiration.

It is a practical way to help sustain and expand the work of creating Scripture-centered articles, Christian teaching, discipleship resources, and encouragement for people who are hungry for biblical truth.
In Philippians 4:15–17, Paul speaks appreciatively of the Philippians' financial partnership in his ministry, while making clear that he sought the spiritual fruit of their generosity.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That last phrase matters.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Rather, if you have the means and believe in this work, you may prayerfully choose to support it as an additional act of Christian generosity.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, worship, obedience, love, service, generosity, and the countless ordinary ways a redeemed life reflects His goodness.
And your contribution helps make it possible for more people to encounter the biblical message that has encouraged you today.
These are simple expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards or a measure of anyone's faith.
The greatest reason to partner with us is the mission itself.
To see more people encounter the truth of Scripture.
To help struggling believers find encouragement rooted in Christ.
To call the wandering back to repentance.
To remind the brokenhearted that forgiveness and restoration are found in Jesus.
And to keep creating resources that nourish faith long after someone finishes reading a Facebook post.

Those resources are available to help believers who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ, learning Scripture, strengthening their spiritual foundations, and becoming more rooted in the truth of the Gospel.
We want the Word of God to remain central.
We want grace to be proclaimed faithfully.
We want discipleship to mean more than emotional excitement that disappears tomorrow.
Invite the believer who has grown weary.
Invite the Christian who has become comfortable with compromise.
Invite the person searching for answers.
Invite even the skeptic who is willing to examine what the Bible actually says.
Because the goal is not merely to build an audience.
It is to point people to Christ.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that may have brought you here.
What if you never receive the complete explanation you have been asking God to give you?
What if the next season still contains unanswered questions?
What if you make the faithful decision and life remains difficult?
What if you pray, obey, wait, and discover that the road is longer than you expected?
Will Jesus still be worthy of your trust?
That is not a question meant to condemn you.
It is an invitation to examine where your confidence truly rests.
Because if your faith depends on knowing exactly how everything will turn out, uncertainty will always have the power to shake you.
But if your faith rests in the crucified and risen Christ, then even unanswered questions do not have to separate you from the love of God.
Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death nor life, nor the powers of the present or the future, nor anything else in creation can separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Even the future you cannot see.
Even the tomorrow you are afraid to face.
Even the season you wish you could skip.
You may not understand every part of your story.
But you can know the Savior to whom you have entrusted your life.
And maybe tonight, instead of asking God to reveal every turn in the road, your prayer can be simpler.
“Lord Jesus, I am afraid.
I want answers You have not given me.
I want guarantees You have not promised.
Sometimes I have confused my need for control with my desire for wisdom.
Forgive me for the ways I have resisted Your truth.
Teach me to trust Your Word.
Give me discernment where the way is unclear.
Give me courage where obedience is clear.
Keep me from recklessness, pride, and decisions driven by fear.
Help me listen to godly counsel.
Help me accept that I am not You, and I do not have to know everything You know.
Thank You for dying for my sins and rising again.
Thank You that my salvation rests in Your grace, not my ability to navigate life perfectly.
And when tomorrow comes, help me take the next faithful step.
Not because I understand everything.
But because I belong to You.
In Your name, Jesus.
Amen.”
If you prayed that sincerely, do not rush past it.
Sit with the truth of what you have just asked.
Maybe nothing around you has changed yet.
The decision may still be waiting.
The bills may still be there.
The uncertainty may still feel heavy.
But you can begin again with the truth God has already given you.
You can repent where repentance is needed.
You can seek wisdom where wisdom is needed.
You can wait where waiting is wise.
And you can obey where His Word has made the path clear.
You do not need to pretend the future is easy.
You do not need to claim that everything will happen exactly as you hope.
You do not need to know the entire road to take a faithful step.
Abraham went out without knowing where he was going.
And the God who called him was faithful to His promise.
Today, we stand on this side of the cross and the empty tomb.
We know the name of the promised Savior.
We know what His grace has accomplished.
We know that He is worthy of our trust.
So when fear whispers, “What if you cannot see what happens next?”
Let faith answer, “I may not see the entire road, but I know the One I am following.”
Share that truth with someone who needs it.
And if you are still struggling, come back to the comments and let someone pray with you.
Because perhaps the most important change in your life today will not be receiving a new explanation.
Perhaps it will be finally surrendering the demand that God explain everything before you trust Him.
The road may still be hidden from your eyes, but the hands that were pierced for you have already shown you the heart of the One you follow.
